Plan Sample Size to Make the Test of a Change in the Squared Multiple Correlation Coefficient Sufficiently Powerful

Source: R/ss_power_R2_change.R
ss_power_R2_change.Rd

Determine the necessary sample size, or the statistical power at a specified sample size, for the model comparison F-test that a set of predictors adds nothing to a regression model that already contains other predictors. The restricted model has p_restricted predictors and the full model adds one or more predictors to it, for p_full in all. The null hypothesis is that the two models have the same population squared multiple correlation coefficient, so that the change in \(R^2\) is zero. This is the test of an increment in \(R^2\) in hierarchical regression (Cohen, Cohen, West, & Aiken, 2003), with the effect size \(f^2\) of Cohen (1988). ss_power_R2 plans the omnibus test of all predictors at once, and ss_power_reg_coef the test of one coefficient with fixed predictors.

Usage

ss_power_R2_change(
  true_R2_full = NULL,
  true_R2_restricted = NULL,
  true_R2_change = NULL,
  true_f2 = NULL,
  p_full,
  p_restricted,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  desired_power = 0.85,
  specified_N = NULL,
  random_predictors = TRUE
)

Arguments

true_R2_full

Population squared multiple correlation coefficient of the outcome with all p_full predictors of the full model, at least 0 and below 1.

true_R2_restricted

Population squared multiple correlation coefficient of the outcome with the p_restricted predictors of the restricted model. The restricted model's predictors are a subset of the full model's, so true_R2_restricted cannot exceed true_R2_full.

true_R2_change

Population change in \(R^2\) when the added predictors join the restricted model, true_R2_full minus true_R2_restricted. It is the squared semipartial correlation of the added predictor when one predictor is added, and the squared multiple semipartial correlation of the added set when several are. Give it with true_R2_full or with true_R2_restricted.

true_f2

Cohen's (1988) effect size for the increment, \(f^2 = (\rho^2_{full} - \rho^2_{restricted}) / (1 - \rho^2_{full})\), a nonnegative number. Give it alone, in place of the \(R^2\) values.

p_full

Number of predictors in the full model, not counting the intercept. A whole number of at least 1.

p_restricted

Number of predictors in the restricted model, not counting the intercept. A whole number from 0 to p_full - 1. Zero is the model with an intercept only, for which the test is the omnibus test of ss_power_R2.

alpha_level

Type I error rate.

desired_power

Desired statistical power, a single number strictly between 0 and 1 (0 and 1 themselves are refused, with a condition of class dmar_desired_power_invalid); used when a sample size is sought. With specified_N the power is computed and desired_power is not used, but a value outside (0, 1) is still refused.

specified_N

Total sample size at which to report power, in place of a search for the necessary sample size. A whole number of at least p_full + 2, the smallest size that leaves an error degree of freedom.

random_predictors

Whether the predictors are treated as random (TRUE, the default) or fixed (FALSE). See Details.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value and nine rows, in this order:

necessary_N

The smallest total sample size at which power is no less than desired_power. When specified_N was given the row is named specified_N and holds that value.

actual_power

Power at that sample size.

noncentral_f_parm

The noncentrality parameter \(N f^2\) under fixed predictors; NA under random predictors, where the power does not come from a single noncentral F with that parameter.

true_f2

The planning value of Cohen's \(f^2\) for the increment: true_f2 as given, or the value the \(R^2\) planning values imply.

true_partial_R2

The population squared multiple partial correlation the planning values imply, \(f^2 / (1 + f^2)\).

true_R2_change

The population change in \(R^2\); NA when true_f2 was given, which does not determine it.

q

The number of predictors removed from the full model to give the restricted model, p_full minus p_restricted: the predictors being tested.

df_1

Numerator degrees of freedom, equal to q.

df_2

Denominator degrees of freedom at the sample size reported, \(N - p_{full} - 1\).

The result carries the dmar_ss_power class, so tidy and glance apply, and the attribute random_predictors records the predictor model.

Details

The effect. Write \(\rho^2_{full}\) and \(\rho^2_{restricted}\) (true_R2_full and true_R2_restricted) for the two population squared multiple correlation coefficients, \(q\) for the number of predictors removed from the full model to give the restricted model (\(q = p_{full} - p_{restricted}\), the predictors being tested; row q of the result, and \(u\) in Cohen, 1988), and \(w\) for the number in the restricted model, p_restricted. In the partial and semipartial correlation functions (var_partial_r, var_semipartial_r, and their planners) \(p\) is p_full, the number of variables partialed out is \(p - q\), and one predictor is of interest, so \(q = 1\). The change \(\rho^2_{full} - \rho^2_{restricted}\) is the squared multiple correlation of the outcome with the part of the added predictors that the restricted model's predictors do not explain: the squared multiple semipartial correlation of the added set (Cohen et al., 2003, Section 5.4.3), and with one added predictor its squared semipartial correlation (Kelley & Maxwell, 2008, Equation 20, p. 176; Aloe & Becker, 2012, Equation 1). So the answer to whether the change in \(R^2\) is the squared semipartial correlation is yes, for one added predictor, and for a set it is the multiple version of the same quantity. Dividing the change by \(1 - \rho^2_{restricted}\) gives the squared multiple partial correlation (the squared partial correlation for one added predictor). Cohen's effect size divides the change by the full model's unexplained variance, $$f^2 = \frac{\rho^2_{full} - \rho^2_{restricted}}{1 - \rho^2_{full}},$$ which is also the squared multiple partial correlation divided by one minus itself. Power depends on the two \(R^2\) values only through \(f^2\), so the ways of giving the effect are equivalent and exactly one is given: any two of the three \(R^2\) quantities (true_R2_full, true_R2_restricted, true_R2_change), or true_f2 alone. The same change is a larger effect when the full model explains more: a change of .05 is \(f^2 = .071\) when the full model explains .30 and \(f^2 = .25\) when it explains .80.

The test. The statistic is $$F = \frac{(R^2_{full} - R^2_{restricted}) / q}{(1 - R^2_{full}) / (N - p_{full} - 1)},$$ with \(q\) and \(N - p_{full} - 1\) degrees of freedom (the form of Cohen et al., 2003, Equation 5.5.1), the general model comparison F of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027, Chapter 3) applied to the two regression models. With one added predictor it is the square of the t-statistic of that predictor's coefficient. In the notation of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027), the restricted model has \(df_R = N - p_{restricted} - 1\) error degrees of freedom and the full model \(df_F = N - p_{full} - 1\); the numerator degrees of freedom are \(df_R - df_F = q\) (rows q and df_1), and the denominator degrees of freedom are \(df_F\) (row df_2). The function takes the numbers of predictors, since the error degrees of freedom depend on the sample size being planned. A categorical predictor with a levels counts as a - 1 predictors.

Fixed predictors. When the predictor values are held constant in hypothetical replications of the study, F follows a noncentral F distribution with \(q\) and \(N - p_{full} - 1\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality \(\lambda = N f^2\), where the \(R^2\) values are those of the design itself (computed from the design's sums of squares, with divisor \(N\)). The calculation is exact under normal errors. With one added predictor this is the square of the noncentrality of Kelley and Maxwell (2008, Equations 16 and 19, p. 175, and Equation 31, p. 181), who give \(\lambda_j = f_j \sqrt{N}\) for the t-test of one coefficient with fixed predictors. That is the noncentrality of ss_power_reg_coef, whose power this function reproduces when one predictor is added: the noncentral t of that function has noncentrality \(\sqrt{N} f\), whose square is \(N f^2\). For any number of added predictors \(N f^2\) is also the noncentrality of ss_power_R2 with fixed predictors.

Random predictors. When the predictors are sampled along with the outcome from a multivariate normal population, the sample squared multiple partial correlation of the outcome with the \(q\) added predictors, given the \(w\) others, has the distribution that a sample squared multiple correlation has with \(q\) predictors and a sample size of \(N - w\) (Gatsonis & Sampson, 1989, p. 518). The critical value is the same as with fixed predictors, since under the null hypothesis the statistic has the central F distribution in both models; only the power differs. The power is computed from that distribution with the noncentral F approximation of Lee (1971, Section 5.1) that ss_power_R2 and ci_R2 use. Against the exact distribution, the power by Lee's approximation differed by at most .0043 over the combinations examined (squared partial correlations up to .95, alpha_level from .001 to .10, and one or more error degrees of freedom) and by at most .0004 with 25 or more error degrees of freedom; the necessary sample size differed from the one the exact distribution gives, by one case, in 20 of 1,500 searches, and in those the power by the exact distribution at the size returned was within .0011 of desired_power. At the levels of power used in planning, power is lower and the necessary sample size larger than with fixed predictors, and the difference grows with the number of predictors in the restricted model relative to the sample size. When power is very low the order can reverse by a small amount (at most .0005 in 1,920 combinations examined, all with no predictors in the restricted model, alpha_level of .001, and power below .09). Predictors are random in most studies in the behavioral, educational, and social sciences, so random_predictors = TRUE is the default.

Relation to the test of one regression coefficient. With one added predictor and random_predictors = FALSE this function and ss_power_reg_coef plan the same test and return the same sample size and power; true_R2_Y_X there is true_R2_full here and true_R2_Y_X_without_j is true_R2_restricted, with p equal to p_full and p_restricted = p_full - 1. ss_power_reg_coef() has fixed predictors only, so with the default of this function (random predictors) the sample size here is larger: 56 against 50 for a change from .30 to .40 with five predictors and power .80 (50 is the example of Kelley & Maxwell, 2008, pp. 181–182). The two functions report the effect size differently: true_f2 here is \(f^2\), and true_f there is \(f\).

Cohen's (1988) noncentrality. Cohen computes power from \(\lambda = f^2 (u + v + 1)\), with \(u\) the number of predictors tested (\(q\) here) and \(v\) the error degrees of freedom (as given by Maxwell, 2000, Equation 1). For the omnibus test \(q + v + 1 = N\). For an increment \(v = N - q - w - 1\), so Cohen's noncentrality is \(f^2 (N - w)\), smaller than \(N f^2\) by \(w f^2\). Cohen's value equals the fixed-predictor calculation for \(q\) predictors, no restricted model, and specified_N set to \(N - w\), and the last example reproduces it that way. That \(N - w\) is only the number that makes the noncentrality agree; it is not the study's sample size, which remains \(N\). The necessary sample size by Cohen's noncentrality exceeds the fixed-predictor answer of this function by at most \(w\) cases. Maxwell (2000, p. 436) notes that \(N f^2\) is the noncentrality for fixed predictors and reads Cohen's form as an adjustment toward random predictors; the random-predictor calculation here makes that adjustment from the sampling distribution itself. MBESS's ss.power.R2() with a nonzero Null.R2 computes this quantity when p is given as the number of predictors added: the sample size it reports is Cohen's total sample size less \(w\).

Error from a larger model. The error variance of the test can be taken from a model with further predictors that are not part of the comparison (the Model 2 error of Cohen et al., 2003, Section 5.5.4). With fixed predictors that calculation is obtained by giving true_f2 with the larger model's unexplained variance in its denominator, p_full as the number of predictors in that larger model, and p_restricted as p_full minus the number of predictors tested. Set random_predictors = FALSE for this calculation. The random-predictor calculation is for the comparison of two nested models only.

Edge cases. When the change is zero the null hypothesis is true: at a specified_N the power returned is alpha_level, and a search stops with an error of class dmar_effect_zero, because no sample size attains desired_power. A specified_N below p_full + 2 leaves no error degrees of freedom and is an error, as is one that is not a whole number. With p_restricted = 0 the restricted model explains nothing, so true_R2_restricted, if given, must be 0 and true_R2_change, if given, must equal true_R2_full; the result is then that of ss_power_R2. A search starts at p_full + 2 and returns that size when it already attains desired_power. The search does not go beyond a sample size of ten million and stops with an error when the power is not attained by then. R computes the noncentral F distribution accurately for a noncentrality parameter up to about one million and warns beyond it; no power is returned from an evaluation at which R gave that warning, and the error says so.

Estimation. To plan for a narrow confidence interval rather than for power when one predictor is added, see ss_aipe_semipartial_r; its true_r_sp squared is true_R2_change and its p is p_full (that function counts the predictor of interest and the variables partialed from it, and one predictor is added, so p_restricted + 1 = p_full). DMAR has no accuracy in parameter estimation planner for the change in \(R^2\) from a set of predictors.

Note

The sample size returned is the smallest whole number at which power is no less than desired_power, so actual_power is slightly above the target. With random predictors that power is the one Lee's approximation gives; the paragraph on random predictors in Details says how closely that approximation follows the exact distribution.

References

Aloe, A. M., & Becker, B. J. (2012). An effect size for regression predictors in meta-analysis. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 37(2), 278–297. doi:10.3102/1076998610396901

Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum. (See Chapter 9.)

Cohen, J., Cohen, P., West, S. G., & Aiken, L. S. (2003). Applied multiple regression/correlation analysis for the behavioral sciences (3rd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum. (See Sections 5.4 and 5.5.)

Gatsonis, C., & Sampson, A. R. (1989). Multiple correlation: Exact power and sample size calculations. Psychological Bulletin, 106(3), 516–524.

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2008). Sample size planning with applications to multiple regression: Power and accuracy for omnibus and targeted effects. In P. Alasuutari, L. Bickman, & J. Brannen (Eds.), The Sage handbook of social research methods (pp. 166–192). Sage.

Lee, Y. S. (1971). Some results on the sampling distribution of the multiple correlation coefficient. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 33(1), 117–130.

Maxwell, S. E. (2000). Sample size and multiple regression analysis. Psychological Methods, 5(4), 434–458. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.5.4.434

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on the general form of the model comparison F-test.)

Examples

# Five predictors are expected to explain .25 of the variance and four
# added predictors to raise that to .30. Necessary sample size for power
# .80 at alpha .01, with random predictors (the default).
ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_restricted = .25, true_R2_full = .30,
                   p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9, alpha_level = .01,
                   desired_power = .80)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       250  
#>  actual_power      0.802
#>  noncentral_f_parm <NA> 
#>  true_f2           0.071
#>  true_partial_R2   0.067
#>  true_R2_change    0.050
#>  q                 4    
#>  df_1              4    
#>  df_2              240  

# The same plan with predictors fixed by design.
ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_restricted = .25, true_R2_full = .30,
                   p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9, alpha_level = .01,
                   desired_power = .80, random_predictors = FALSE)
#>  term              value 
#>  necessary_N       242   
#>  actual_power      0.802 
#>  noncentral_f_parm 17.286
#>  true_f2           0.071 
#>  true_partial_R2   0.067 
#>  true_R2_change    0.050 
#>  q                 4     
#>  df_1              4     
#>  df_2              232   

# The effect given as the change with the full model's value, and as
# Cohen's f squared. Power at a sample size of 90, fixed predictors.
ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_change = .05, true_R2_full = .30,
                   p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9, alpha_level = .01,
                   specified_N = 90, random_predictors = FALSE)
#>  term              value
#>  specified_N       90   
#>  actual_power      0.241
#>  noncentral_f_parm 6.429
#>  true_f2           0.071
#>  true_partial_R2   0.067
#>  true_R2_change    0.050
#>  q                 4    
#>  df_1              4    
#>  df_2              80   
ss_power_R2_change(true_f2 = .05 / .70, p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9,
                   alpha_level = .01, specified_N = 90,
                   random_predictors = FALSE)
#>  term              value
#>  specified_N       90   
#>  actual_power      0.241
#>  noncentral_f_parm 6.429
#>  true_f2           0.071
#>  true_partial_R2   0.067
#>  true_R2_change    <NA> 
#>  q                 4    
#>  df_1              4    
#>  df_2              80   

# The effect given as the restricted model's value and the change, the
# way a hierarchical regression is often described. Random predictors.
ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_restricted = .25, true_R2_change = .05,
                   p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9, alpha_level = .01,
                   desired_power = .80)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       250  
#>  actual_power      0.802
#>  noncentral_f_parm <NA> 
#>  true_f2           0.071
#>  true_partial_R2   0.067
#>  true_R2_change    0.050
#>  q                 4    
#>  df_1              4    
#>  df_2              240  

# One added predictor with fixed predictors is the test of its regression
# coefficient: the two functions return the same sample size.
ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_restricted = .30, true_R2_full = .40,
                   p_restricted = 4, p_full = 5, desired_power = .80,
                   random_predictors = FALSE)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       50   
#>  actual_power      0.806
#>  noncentral_f_parm 8.333
#>  true_f2           0.167
#>  true_partial_R2   0.143
#>  true_R2_change    0.100
#>  q                 1    
#>  df_1              1    
#>  df_2              44   
ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = .40, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = .30, p = 5,
                  desired_power = .80)
#>  term              value
#>  necessary_N       50   
#>  actual_power      0.806
#>  noncentral_t_parm 2.887
#>  true_f            0.408

# Cohen's (1988) noncentrality for the design of the third example,
# f squared times (N - w) with w = 5: four predictors and no restricted
# model, with specified_N set to 90 - 5 so the noncentrality matches
# Cohen's. The study's sample size is still 90.
ss_power_R2_change(true_f2 = .05 / .70, p_restricted = 0, p_full = 4,
                   alpha_level = .01, specified_N = 85,
                   random_predictors = FALSE)
#>  term              value
#>  specified_N       85   
#>  actual_power      0.223
#>  noncentral_f_parm 6.071
#>  true_f2           0.071
#>  true_partial_R2   0.067
#>  true_R2_change    <NA> 
#>  q                 4    
#>  df_1              4    
#>  df_2              80
